newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. environment agency negotiates budget.
newsitem.headline: U.N. environment agency negotiates budget.

text.p: Officials from 100 governments started talks on Wednesday on a new two-year budget for the U.N. environment agency, already under attack from the United States as "disjointed, inefficient and in a state of crisis".
The officials are attending a two-week session of the Governing Council of the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP), the agency's top legislative and policy organ.

Conference officials said delegates would consider three budget options for the two-year period: $130 million, $105 million and $80 million. The agreed budget is to be presented to environment ministers next week for approval.
But experts doubted that rich donors led by Washington would agree to even the lowest figure.
"It is highly doubtful that the Council will persuade donors to pay for a budget anywhere near $80 million. The will seems to be lacking," an African diplomat told Reuters.

Central to UNEP's financial crisis is U.S. reluctance to increase funding to the global environment watchdog. The Americans are calling for budget cuts and reforms they say are essential in revitalising UNEP, which is based in Nairobi.
On Tuesday a U.S. delegate led the onslaught on UNEP, calling it "disjointed and inefficient" and describing its governing structure, programmes and administration as needing "comprehensive reform".
The United States made clear there would be no extra funding until its demands were met.

Diplomats at the meeting, held every two years to approve a programme for managing natural resources and improving the environment, said the U.S. attacks appeared to be directed at the management style of its executive director, Elizabeth Dowdeswell, a Canadian.
Dowdeswell on Monday lamented the budget cuts called for by the United States, saying they were undermining UNEP's ability to manage the environment.
She said she had made huge strides in streamlining UNEP while cutting costs.
China has thrown its weight behind developing countries seeking increased aid for UNEP. These countries accuse the West of a hidden agenda in demanding reforms before paying dues.
"The U.S. and those who owe the U.N. money must be made to pay first before they put forward unrealistic opinions that lack support," Kenya's Standard newspaper said in an editorial.
UNEP has seen its budget drop sharply over the last few years as donors linked funding to reforms.
From $160 million during 1991-92, the budget fell to $105 million in the last two years and even then only $62.5 million was disbursed by donors.
New U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has promised to reform the entire U.N. system.
Washington vetoed a further term for his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, accusing him of failure to press reform of the 185-nation organisation.
Western governments say the U.N. agency has appeared less effective since the 1992 Earth Summit in Brazil.
The summit, the U.N. Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), gathered world leaders in Rio de Janiero, where they made fresh commitments to environmental protection.

Western governments want UNEP, the only global U.N. agency based in the developing world, to refocus on core tasks -- monitoring the state of the planet, identifying emerging issues, initiating global responses and promoting development of international law.
